You're right, they collapse. `async_config_entry_first_refresh()` differs only by raising `ConfigEntryNotReady` instead of reporting through `last_update_success` — and since Modbus is optional here, that exception was caught two lines later and turned back into a bool. Now it refreshes, checks, and lets the entry state decide the dispatch on its own:

```python
await coordinator.async_refresh()
if not coordinator.last_update_success:
    return False
# Only for re-scans. Initial setup adds entities through the
# platforms' async_setup_entry.
if self.config_entry.state is ConfigEntryState.LOADED:
    async_dispatcher_send(self.hass, SOLAR_NET_DISCOVERY_NEW, coordinator)
return True
```

One behaviour does change, and I think for the better: a failed first refresh is now logged by the coordinator instead of being swallowed. It should be rare, since the coordinator is only created after `discover()` already succeeded against the device.

author: agners
body:
One case I'd like us to handle: `discovery.json` is Supervisor-internal state and isn't part of a backup — backups cover `homeassistant`, `share`, `addons/local`, `ssl` and `media`. So restoring onto a new system gives the app a fresh discovery uuid while the restored config entry still holds the old one. The URL is unchanged, so the flow aborts on the URL match and the entry keeps a uuid that no longer exists anywhere in Supervisor. Uninstalling the app then leaves the entry behind (`async_process_del` matches on `unique_id`), and the entry's `discovery_keys` are stale too, so re-discovery on removal is broken as well.

That's the normal migrate-to-new-hardware path, so I'd rather not leave it. Wyoming handles the equivalent case by re-linking the entry:

```python
for entry in self._iter_entries(uri.hostname, uri.port):
    return self.async_update_reload_and_abort(
        entry,
        unique_id=discovery_info.uuid,
        reload_even_if_entry_is_unchanged=False,
        reason="already_configured",
    )
```

Suggestion, combined with the reordering in the other thread:

```python
await self.async_set_unique_id(discovery_info.uuid)
self._abort_if_unique_id_configured(updates={CONF_URL: url})

# A restore onto a new system gives the app a new discovery uuid while the
# restored entry still holds the old one. Re-link it so that Supervisor can
# still remove the entry together with the app.
for entry in self._async_current_entries(include_ignore=False):
    if entry.source == SOURCE_HASSIO and entry.data.get(CONF_URL) == url:
        return self.async_update_reload_and_abort(
            entry,
            unique_id=discovery_info.uuid,
            reload_even_if_entry_is_unchanged=False,
            reason="already_configured",
        )

self._async_abort_entries_match({CONF_URL: url})
```

Note the `SOURCE_HASSIO` gate, which is where I'd deviate from Wyoming: a manually created entry can't be fully adopted anyway, since `async_update_entry` can't change `source` and `async_process_del` requires it. Re-linking one would leave it half-managed — uuid updated but still not removable — which seems worse than leaving it alone. Gated this way, adoption is all-or-nothing: complete for entries that were already Supervisor-managed, no-op for everything else.

Worth a test: existing entry with the old uuid, discovery arrives with a new uuid and the same URL, assert `already_configured` and that the entry now carries the new uuid.

I do think Supervisor should also keep discovery state in backups — most likely alongside the app metadata so it is restored together with the app, plus pruning of stale messages when an app's config changes. I'll follow up on that separately. But that only helps backups taken after such a fix, so Core should cope regardless.

On the side: `uptime_kuma` and `pyload` use exactly the same uuid-as-unique-id pattern and have the same gap, so whatever we settle on here is probably worth porting to those two later. Not something this PR needs to solve.

author: agners
body:
Fair point on the update path — with a new URL, line 210 can't match, so line 212 is reached exactly when it has work to do.

I'd still swap them, because "the same discovery info arrives again" isn't hypothetical. Verified locally: with the config entry deleted and the app left running, restarting Core loads `mcp` at `EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_START` and re-runs this flow, without Supervisor pushing anything — `_async_discovery_start_handler` in `homeassistant/components/hassio/discovery.py` replays the stored message on every start. So an unchanged discovery message reaching this flow again is the normal case, not an edge case, and today it aborts on the data match at line 210 before the identity check at line 212 is ever reached.

With the order swapped:
- the abort happens on identity rather than on a data field, which is the semantically correct match here;
- an entry sitting in `SETUP_RETRY` gets reloaded instead of waiting out its backoff (the `elif self.source in DISCOVERY_SOURCES` branch of `_abort_if_unique_id_configured`);
- `flow.unique_id` is set, so `async_finish_flow` can refresh the entry's `discovery_keys`.

`_async_abort_entries_match()` then stays as the fallback for entries that don't carry the uuid, which is where it belongs.

Supervisor does currently suppress the app-restart re-announce (`Discovery.send()` returns early when the config is unchanged), but I don't think Core should rely on that — a repeated discovery message should be handled gracefully on our side either way.

The device class is fixed per parameter but the unit comes from the API, and HA only accepts certain units per device class (`DEVICE_CLASS_UNITS`). PM1/PM10/PM2.5 accept only µg/m³ and CO2 only ppm, so a sensor reporting anything else would be created with an invalid unit and trigger HA's "not a valid unit for the device class" warning.

Since this function already decides which sensors exist, I'd filter here: skip a sensor when its parameter has a device class and the normalised unit is not in `DEVICE_CLASS_UNITS[device_class]`. Unsupported parameters can be skipped here too, so `sensor.py` can drop its `if parameter in SENSOR_DESCRIPTIONS` check and create one entity per key. The same helper can back `_supported_parameters` in the config flow so a station is not offered when its only supported sensor has an unusable unit.

To avoid a circular import (`sensor.py` imports this module), move the parameter to device class mapping into `const.py` and build `SENSOR_DESCRIPTIONS` from it. That also removes the `from .sensor import SENSOR_DESCRIPTIONS` in `config_flow.py`.

This queries every radius returned by `_search_radii` unconditionally, so a submit with the default 25 km radius always makes three API requests (5, 10, 25 km) whose result sets are nested supersets of each other, and then only ten options are shown. Three requests per submit is a noticeable share of the 60 requests per minute budget, especially since the user can resubmit after moving the map.

The test name `test_location_subentry_map_flow_expands_radius_for_useful_locations` suggests the intent was to expand only when the smaller radius does not yield enough useful stations. If that is the intent, implement it: iterate the radii and stop as soon as the collected useful (supported and not yet configured) locations reach `MAX_LOCATION_OPTIONS`. That means the filtering has to move into this function or the loop has to be driven from the flow step, since usefulness is decided after the response comes back. Then add the negative test case where the 5 km query already yields enough locations and `locations.list` is called exactly once.

If the staged radii instead exist to work around the 100 result page cap with no distance ordering, then please add a one line comment saying so, because the code does not explain why one 25 km query is not enough.

author: Markus98
body: Only page 1 with `limit=100` is fetched and no `order_by` is passed. The SDK exposes `order_by` and `sort_order`, but the API does not document ordering by distance, so in a dense area with more than 100 locations inside a radius the nearest stations can be missing from the result. The smaller radii mitigate this, which is another reason to keep them but to make the expansion conditional rather than always running all three. Worth a comment either way, since the 100 cap is the actual constraint driving the design.

author: Markus98
body:
(Potential slop below)

I think the geometric elevation is right for the `ELEVATION_HORIZON` comparisons, but not here. The premise in the comment doesn't hold for astral 2.2: `time_of_transit()` solves for `requested_zenith + refraction_at_zenith(requested_zenith)`, so `dawn`/`dusk` with a given depression return the moment the *apparent* (refracted) elevation equals `-depression`. The geometric elevation at that moment is lower by the refraction (civil dawn: apparent -6.003, geometric -6.057; golden hour top +6: apparent 6.000, geometric 5.859).

The dawn/dusk/golden hour/blue hour triggers schedule via astral with `depression=-elevation`, so they fire on apparent elevation. With this change `is_night`, `is_morning_twilight`, `is_evening_twilight`, `is_golden_hour` and `is_blue_hour` no longer agree with their own triggers. Measured with the repo's astral:

| trigger firing | condition flips, apparent (before) | condition flips, geometric (after) |
|---|---|---|
| civil dawn, 52°N equinox | +2 s | +23 s |
| civil dawn, 70°N January | +1 s | +58 s |
| golden hour ended (+6°), 52°N | 0 s | +56 s |
| civil dusk, 52°N | +1 s | -20 s (already False when trigger fires) |

So "trigger: dawn (civil), condition: is_morning_twilight (civil)" would fail after this PR.

Suggest keeping the default (refracted) elevation in `_solar_position()` and only using `with_refraction=False` where the value is compared against `ELEVATION_HORIZON`. The same reasoning applies to the `phase is None` fallback in entity.py, though the impact there is only the polling interval.

Side note: astral's effective geometric horizon is `-(SUN_APPARENT_RADIUS + refraction_at_zenith(90 + SUN_APPARENT_RADIUS))` ≈ -0.789°, not -0.833°, so the const.py comment saying -0.833 is "the value astral uses" isn't accurate either. Deriving the constant from astral would make the horizon comparisons match sunrise/sunset exactly.

Okay so I have seen this case before, in for example switchbot and bsblan and I have discussed it before so a few thoughts that we considered back then:
- date times are meh because they'd always update, so they would always have a state update
- automatic date time sync is weird. It's something you forget and it's something that happens quite "invisible". So imagine resetting your CMOS battery and then the time is off and NTP doesn't work and then your pool gets a weird time. (Far fetched example, but there probably are different issues as well, docker containers with weird timezones)

So what we decided back then was to have a button which would trigger a time sync to the device. This is traceable, optional and thus is a nice way to expose this functionality

This test and `test_entry_reload_from_migration_error_fails` below both cover the same `OperationNotAllowed` branch, just from different states. Since the method raises before touching the integration, the `mock_integration`/`mock_platform` setup and the `async_*` mocks are not needed for the failure path either.

Suggest merging them into one test parametrized over `state`, similar to `test_entry_reload_error` further down:

```python
@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "state",
    [
        config_entries.ConfigEntryState.NOT_LOADED,
        config_entries.ConfigEntryState.LOADED,
        config_entries.ConfigEntryState.SETUP_ERROR,
        config_entries.ConfigEntryState.FAILED_UNLOAD,
    ],
)
async def test_async_retry_migration_with_incorrect_state(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    manager: config_entries.ConfigEntries,
    state: config_entries.ConfigEntryState,
) -> None:
    """Test async_retry_migration raises when the entry is not in MIGRATION_ERROR."""
    entry = MockConfigEntry(domain="comp", state=state)
    entry.add_to_hass(hass)

    with pytest.raises(config_entries.OperationNotAllowed, match=str(state)):
        await manager.async_retry_migration(entry.entry_id)

    assert entry.state is state
```

author: arturpragacz
body:
For dict/list subclasses the generated validator doesn't rebuild at all. probatio's compiled mapping prologue is `if type(data) is not dict: return _interpreted(data)`, and the compiled sequence path bails on anything that isn't exactly `list`. So for `NodeDictClass`/`NodeListClass` both policies run the same interpreted rebuild.

Keeping the parametrization is fine since it guards that bail-out, but the docstring shouldn't claim the two policies rebuild through separate code paths.

body:
Thanks! Few comments but seems fine overall. Two more things:

Removing `@cache` is definitely correct IMO, but it was likely intentionally added there in the first place. From the PR description:
 > The function only runs for Matter devices during a Google Assistant sync, and the lookup is cheap.

I think it's probably fine to remove, but I do want to note that the Google Assistant integration calls this [once **per entity**](https://github.com/home-assistant/core/blob/c314545d0ae0ea4894c410631771d96479a22766/homeassistant/components/google_assistant/helpers.py#L585-L586) when doing a sync. And the [lookup in the Matter integration is linear](https://github.com/home-assistant/core/blob/c314545d0ae0ea4894c410631771d96479a22766/homeassistant/components/matter/helpers.py#L115-L123), so you'll end up with `O(entities * nodes * endpoints)` now. This could maybe take a few hundred milliseconds for huge setups, though likely only about 1 ms for normal/big setups.

Should Matter maybe cache some info in `entry.runtime_data`? (Or have a `get_matter_device_infos(hass)` helper which just returns the whole `device_id -> MatterDeviceInfo` mapping in one call, and Google Assistant calls once per whole sync request? (not per entity sync))

---

And there's also one behavioral change, which likely shouldn't matter: When a sync was done while the Matter integration is loaded, and it is then later unloaded (e.g. because Matter Server add-on/app is updating), and another sync occurs at that time, the extra metadata would be missing then. Before, `@cache` returned the old data.

Thanks for the PR! The change itself goes in the right direction, but the bug it describes doesn't happen, so the framing needs fixing and the cleanup is only half done.

`ConfigEntry._async_init_reauth` doesn't pass the entry data as is. It merges in the data the caller provides: `self.data | (data or {})`. Broadlink's only reauth trigger, in `device.py`, passes the name on purpose:

`self.config.async_start_reauth(self.hass, data={CONF_NAME: self.name})`

And `self.name` is the config entry title. So `CONF_NAME` is present in `entry_data` on the only path that starts a reauth, and there is no `KeyError` in practice. Reading the name straight from the entry title is still a good change: one source of truth instead of a round trip through the reauth data. But then please finish it:

- `tests/components/broadlink/test_config_flow.py`: remove `data={"name": device.name}` from the existing `start_reauth_flow` calls.

author: Markus98
body:
Dropping every entry that has a live state also drops entries that were just written by `async_restore_entity_removed`, before the entity's state is gone from the state machine.

In `Entity.__async_remove_impl` the order is: `async_internal_will_remove_from_hass` (stores the live state into `last_states` and removes the entity from `self.entities`), then `await self.async_will_remove_from_hass()`, and only after that the state is removed. If a dump runs during that await, the entry is dropped and the re-added entity gets `None` from `async_get_last_state()`. Before this PR the entry survived in memory, so a reload still restored.

Example: reloading an automation that has a running action with a `delay:` step. `AutomationEntity.async_will_remove_from_hass` awaits the script to stop, which can take the whole delay. If the 15 minute dump fires in that window, the reloaded automation loses its enabled/disabled state and `last_triggered`.

Only dropping entries that were just replaced by a fresh `StoredState` from a registered entity avoids this, while keeping the disk output identical:

```python
            if entity_id in current_states_by_entity_id:
                # Keep entries not backed by a registered entity, e.g. an
                # entity that is being removed and will be re-added
                if entity_id not in self.entities:
                    last_states[entity_id] = stored_state
                continue
```

`gh aw compile` warns that this workflow has no `concurrency.job-discriminator`, so the generated `conclusion` job uses a single concurrency group (`gh-aw-conclusion-quality-scale-reviewer`) shared by every run of this workflow, dispatched or not. ```suggestion
concurrency:

  cancel-in-progress: true
  job-discriminator: ${{ github.run_id }}

The reset is gated on the closure's own `power` dict, so it misses the value the entity restored from the previous run. `TeslemetryStreamSensorEntity` is a `RestoreSensor` and restores its last native value before this listener is registered. If Home Assistant restarts mid-session and the session then ends with only a `DetailedChargeState` message (the PR description says a final zero power is not reliably sent), `power` is still `{None, None}`, the guard is false, and the sensor keeps the restored charging power indefinitely.

Reproduced by seeding a restored `148.2` with `mock_restore_cache_with_extra_data`, setting up the platform and sending only `DetailedChargeStateDisconnected`:

```
AssertionError: assert '148.2' == '0'
```

Resetting on the charging transition instead of on stored power fixes it and is equivalent for the existing parametrized cases, since `_update` already zeroes values while not charging:

```suggestion
    def _update_charging(state: str | None) -> None:
        nonlocal charging
        was_charging = charging
        charging = state in {"Starting", "Charging"}
        if was_charging and not charging:
            power["ac"] = power["dc"] = 0
            callback(0)
```

A test covering the restore case would be good too.

We really like timestamps, mostly because those are _always_ correct. As in, if your entity updates every 30 seconds, then it's correct for a single seconds and off for 29 seconds. So by transforming that in a timestamp, we come to a point where it's always correct. This also avoid us writing toooo many states (as it would otherwise write state every update, and now only once) (we have ways to ignore variance, so we avoid writing too much state here too).

Hence the question if it could be paused, because if it can, the number would stay the same and we'd have to update the timestamp every time.

So to me this sounds like a good usecase for the timestamp. We can split this one off from this PR if you want to

body:
Thanks for pulling zizmor into its own workflow, getting findings into Code Scanning is a good move. I do have a few concerns before this can go in. I ran zizmor 1.30.1 against the PR head to verify the first three.

**Blocking**

1. **The file-wide `template-injection` ignore hides real injections** (`.github/zizmor.yml:12`). I added `run: echo "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_branch }}"` to `check-requirements.lock.yml`. Without the config zizmor flags it as an error, with the config it reports nothing. That is the `workflow_run` triggered agent workflow, which has secrets. The three current instances are informational, so please ignore them by exact location (like `check-requirements.lock.yml:694:9`) instead. The same applies to `ref-version-mismatch` on line 9: it is a tamper signal, and this ignores it for every action that ever lands in that file.

2. **The gate is weaker than what it replaces** (`.github/workflows/zizmor.yml:71`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml:26`). The old CI job ran `--pedantic` without a severity floor, so any finding failed. With `min-severity: medium`, a job adding an undocumented `pull-requests: write` now passes and only shows up in Code Scanning after merge. Same for `anonymous-definition`, `concurrency-limits` and `ref-version-mismatch`. Can we keep the PR gate at the old strictness?

3. **Line:col ignores in a generated file** (`.github/zizmor.yml:20-22`). Shifting the lock file by a single line brings back both High findings (`unsound-condition` at 82, `github-env` at 436) and fails the gate. Since the lock-file `exclude` is also gone from the pre-commit hook, it fails locally too. Every `gh aw compile` that touches anything above those lines means hand-relocating them.

Related to 3: the `unsound-condition` finding is real. The fork guard `if: >` on line 81 always evaluates to true, because the folded scalar leaves a trailing newline. If we suppress it, please link an upstream issue so we know when to drop the ignore.

**Should fix**

- The PR gate runs with online audits on (action default). A new GHSA or a moved tag for an action in some unrelated workflow then fails every PR touching workflows, and the local hook can't reproduce it. I'd set `online-audits: false` on the gate and keep online audits in the report job.
- The relevance pathspec and `push.paths` miss `**/action.yml`, `**/action.yaml` and `.pre-commit-hooks.yaml`, which zizmor does audit.
- The Renovate custom manager bumps the zizmor `version:` from PyPI, but zizmor-action only accepts versions it ships in its support table. A PyPI release ahead of an action release breaks the gate with "Unknown version". The regex also silently stops matching if a key lands between `uses:` and `with:`.
- The report job hands a `security-events: write` token to the zizmor container, which only needs read for online audits. Splitting the SARIF upload into its own job fixes that.
- `master` and `rc` have no scheduled run, and the push `paths` filter is subject to the 300-file diff limit, so release merges can skip the scan and leave their alerts stale.

**Nits**

- The path list is duplicated (`push.paths` and the `git diff` pathspec) and both include dependabot files that don't exist. `dorny/paths-filter` is already used in `ci.yaml`.
- Every PR gets a runner plus a full checkout just to run `git diff`, while the check isn't required.
- `fetch-depth: 2` in the report job, the explicit `config`/`--config` (zizmor discovers `.github/zizmor.yml` itself) and `collect: all` are redundant.
- The PR job is called "(code scanning)" but has `advanced-security: false`.
- The Renovate group and GitHub Actions allowlist descriptions now contradict what the config does.
- The report job has no `github.repository_owner == 'home-assistant'` guard, so it runs in forks.

body:
Hooking the restore into `_async_setup` is fragile. Nearly every coordinator subclass in core overrides `_async_setup`, so a subclass of this coordinator that follows that pattern will silently never restore.

Since the store is loaded in bootstrap before any integration is set up, and `async_restore_data` only reads an in-memory dict, we can restore at the end of `__init__` instead. That drops this override and the requirement to call `async_restore_data` manually for coordinators that don't use `async_config_entry_first_refresh`.

One thing to call out in the docstring then: subclasses that assign `self.data` in their own `__init__` would shadow the restored data.

author: frenck
body:
The bug this catches is real, but as written it also flags entities that deliberately get their availability somewhere else. I went through all 28 existing hits:

**About 18 are real bugs.** Availability comes purely from `coordinator.data`, which keeps the last good data after a failed update, so the entity stays available with stale values: ccm15, ezviz, motion_blinds (2x), proxmoxve, pvpc_hourly_pricing, scorpiontrack, seventeentrack, starlink, subaru, supla, tado, xbox, yardian, comelit. Also arve (`super()._attr_available` is not `super().available`), and tolo and nibe_heatpump, which use `available` for a state.

**About 10 have their own, deliberate source:**
- Bluetooth connection: eurotronic_cometblue (with a comment explaining why), melnor
- Websocket or push next to polling: husqvarna_automower, overseerr
- The library knows better: devialet (`client.is_available`), dwd_weather_warnings (`api.data_valid`)
- Own tracking through `_attr_available`: modbus, paperless_ngx
- Per sensor by design: goodwe
- Unclear: simplisafe

A third false positives is too much for a warning, especially since it mostly hits new integrations.

Suggestion: narrow it down instead of dropping it. Only flag when the override takes its availability solely from coordinator data: `self.coordinator.data...`, or entity properties that read `coordinator.data` themselves (such as `self.data` or `self._zone_object`; astroid can follow those getters). As soon as the body uses anything else (a client, device, websocket, `self._attr_available`), stay quiet. That keeps the 18 real bugs and drops the 10 deliberate cases. Anyone still flagged with a genuine other source adds a disable with a comment, which documents the intent too.
